phonemes.desc: Dental nasal [n], short close [i], then the f voiced to [v] between voiced sounds — Old Norse wrote f but heard v, as in modern Icelandic Niflheimur — and a clear [l].

Voiceless [h], the falling diphthong [ɛi] (Old Norse ei, as in modern 'hay' gliding down), bilabial [m], and the final syllabic nominative [r̩] — the masculine -r ending, sounded as its own light beat.

pronunciation.approximation: NIVL-haym-r — the f is soft, sounding as v; the second element glides like 'aim' with an h in front; end with a light trilled r that carries its own syllable.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: niflheimr, the masculine compound 'mist-world'; the manuscript form, unchanged since the Eddas.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Niflheimur, the learned word for the primordial mist-world, kept alive from the medieval corpus.

kin.label: Old Norse near-kin
kin.form: niflhel 'mist-Hel', the poetic word for the world below Hel — Vafþrúðnismál 43 and Baldrs draumar 2 use it where the prose says Niflheimr.

kin.label: Indo-European kin
kin.form: Latin nebula, Greek nephélē 'cloud', Sanskrit nábhas 'cloud, mist' — the first element descends from the inherited root *nebh- 'cloud, fog'.

pronunciation.note: Niflheimr is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. Only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input; the mist-world was never hard to type, only hard to imagine.

domains.title: The Mist-World Before the World
domains.subtitle: Hvergelmir, the Élivágar, and the Northern Pole of Ginnungagap
domains.lead: Niflheimr is the oldest address in the Norse cosmos: the world of fog and rime that existed, Snorri says, many ages before the earth was made — the cold northern pole of the yawning gap, from whose roaring well every river in creation flows and from whose poisoned ice the first living thing quickened.

cards.name: Hvergelmir
cards.desc: The roaring kettle: the well in Niflheimr's middle, whence Grímnismál says all waters have their course.

cards.name: The Élivágar
cards.desc: The ice-waves: eleven rivers older than the earth — Svöl, Gunnþrá, Fjörm, Fimbulþul, Slíðr, Hríð, Sylgr, Ylgr, Víð, Leiptr, and Gjöll, which runs nearest the gate of Hel.

cards.name: The Rime and the Venom
cards.desc: Frost fog layered across the gap and the yeasty eitr that hardened like dross from a fire — creation's raw material, and its warning.

cards.name: Níðhöggr
cards.desc: The malice-striker: the serpent that gnaws Yggdrasill's third root from below, where it stands over Niflheimr above the well.

symbols.name: Hvergelmir, the roaring kettle
symbols.meaning: The source beneath all sources: every river in the world is one of its children

symbols.name: The Élivágar
symbols.meaning: The ice-waves older than the earth — water carrying the venom that froze into the first flesh

symbols.name: The rime fog
symbols.meaning: Cold as a substance, not an absence: the raw material the warm south breathed on until it lived

mythology.lead: Niflheimr's mythology is the mythology of before: it stars in no adventure and houses no hero, because its story is over before the gods' stories begin — and yet every river, every frost giant, and every corpse that sinks past Hel is still paying its tribute to the mist-world.

myths.title: The World That Came First
myths.text: Snorri's chronology begins not with a god but with a climate. Niflheimr, he says, was made many ages before the earth was created, and in its middle is the well called Hvergelmir, from which flow the rivers: Svöl the cool, Gunnþrá the battle-defiant, Fjörm the swift, Fimbulþul the loud-babbling, Slíðr the fearsome and Hríð the storming, Sylgr and Ylgr, Víð the broad, and Leiptr the flashing — and Gjöll, the resounding, which runs nearest the gate of Hel. Before there was a world to water, the mist-world already had its watershed.

myths.title: The Yeasty Venom and the Quickening
myths.text: The Élivágar ran so far from their source that the yeasty venom in them hardened, like dross running out of a fire, and turned to ice; rime and fog rose layer upon layer across Ginnungagap's northern half, while sparks and molten flecks flew out of Muspellsheimr in the south. Where the warm breath met the rime, the ice thawed and dripped — and the dripping drops quickened into the likeness of a man, named Ymir by the gods and Aurgelmir, the mud-yeller, by the rime-giants who descend from him. The Poetic Edda keeps the same recipe in three lines: out of Élivágar spurted venom-drops, Vafþrúðnismál says, and grew until a giant was made. The first life in the North was brewed from poisoned ice thawed by a fire it could not see.

myths.title: The Root Over the Well
myths.text: When the world was finally built, Niflheimr kept the oldest seat in it. Yggdrasill's third root, Snorri says, extends over Niflheimr, and beneath that root is Hvergelmir, and the serpent Níðhöggr gnaws the root from below — the ash is always being eaten at its oldest corner. Grímnismál completes the water-cycle: the hart Eikþyrnir stands on Valhöll's roof cropping the leaves, and from his horns it drips into Hvergelmir, whence all waters have their course. The rivers of gods and giants alike — the Fjörm and the Slíðr, the Gjöll and the Leiptr — are one well's outflow, and the well sits in the mist.

myths.title: Niflhel, Down in the Ninth World
myths.text: In the poems the mist-world darkens into something lower. Óðinn, proving his wisdom to the giant Vafþrúðnir, says he journeyed through nine worlds below Niflhel; in Baldrs draumar he saddles Sleipnir and rides down to Niflhel to wake a dead seeress and wring the prophecy of Baldr's death from her. Snorri states the grim geography plainly: evil men go to Hel, and thence down to Niflhel — that is down in the ninth world. The world that was first becomes the world that is lowest: creation's old north pole, demoted to the cellar of the dead.

lore.syncretism: Niflheimr needs no borrowing to be explained: its first element is one of the most securely inherited words in the Germanic vocabulary, the same mist that Greek keeps in nephélē, Latin in nebula, and Sanskrit in nábhas — three daughter languages and the North all descended from the same cloud. The genuine scholarly argument is internal. Niflheimr is a prose word: the poems overwhelmingly know niflhel, mist-Hel, and several handbooks treat Snorri's fully mapped Niflheimr — with its well, its eleven rivers, and its place opposite Muspellsheimr — as a thirteenth-century systematization raised on genuinely older material, since Hvergelmir and the Élivágar are Eddic and attested in Grímnismál and Vafþrúðnismál centuries before the Prose Edda. The comparative pattern is common enough: a pole of cold set against a pole of fire at the beginning of things — but the Norse version is unusual in making the cold not merely older than the gods but older than the earth itself.
lore.culturalLegacy: The mist-world's afterlife runs through every retelling that needs a bottom floor for the cosmos. Wagner rebuilt it as Nibelheim, the smoke-filled subterranean forge-realm of Alberich in Das Rheingold — a conflation of Niflheimr with the Nibelung dwarf-lore that no saga ever made, and one of the most consequential mistranslations in myth reception. Modern fantasy keeps the map: Marvel's comics and films count 'Niffleheim' among their Nine Realms, and games from the God of War series to a dozen smaller titles send players trudging through its fog as the endgame of cold. In Iceland the word never needed reviving — Niflheimur is simply the old word, still in service. What survives beneath every adaptation is the Edda's strangest idea: that the first thing was not light but fog, and that everything warm is a late arrival.
lore.extendedMeditation: Niflheimr is the patron of what was here first. Before the gods, before the giants, before the earth itself, there was a world of mist with a well in the middle of it, and rivers already running. The Norse imagination refused to let creation begin with a decree; it began with weather — with frost accumulating in a silence no one had yet named, thawed, at last, by a warmth it never asked for. Every river still runs from that well, which is the myth's way of saying that every living thing is downstream of the cold it rose from.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Niflheimr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the compound would have been carved ᚾᛁᚠᛚᚼᛁᛘᛦ (n-i-f-l-h-i-m-R, the i-rune writing both e and i, the ᛦ carrying the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: niflheimr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Niflheimr is a textual world: it has no cult, no toponym, and no carved witness — unsurprising for a cosmographical term rather than a deity. Its attestation is manuscriptal: Grímnismál and Vafþrúðnismál in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (c. 1270) preserve Hvergelmir and the Élivágar; Baldrs draumar, with its ride down to Niflhel, hangs by the single thread of AM 748 I 4to (early 14th c.); and the fully mapped Niflheimr of Gylfaginning survives in the thirteenth- and fourteenth-century codices of the Prose Edda. No runic inscription records the word, and the image tradition is indirect at most: scholars have been tempted to see the world-tree's serpent-gnawed roots on Scandinavian picture stones and church carvings, but nothing is labelled, and the mist-world itself — a climate, not a figure — was never the kind of thing a Viking Age carver set in stone.
